title: The gurdwaras return, 1925
hookLine: after years of peaceful protest a law hands historic gurdwaras to an elected Sikh body
tomorrow: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars

lines: THE NEXT MORNING, A NEW GROUP.
cards: Every morning, a group of men walks down a country road toward a gurdwara's garden, to cut firewood for its kitchen. Every morning, police stop them and beat them with long sticks. The men don't raise a hand.
They fall, get up if they can, and are carried away. The next morning, a new group walks the same road. And the next.
Visitors come from far away just to watch, and can't believe it.

teach.b: SGPC stands for the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. Shiromani means foremost, supreme; parbandhak means managing.
Sikhs formed it in November 1920, at the Akal Takht, to take the historic shrines back from the mahants and run them for the whole community. At first the government refused to recognize it.
So began years of what Sikhs call morchas, peaceful campaigns.

In the keys affair of 1921, the government took the keys to the Golden Temple's treasury. Sikhs protested without violence, in huge numbers, until the keys were handed back to the Sikh leader Baba Kharak Singh.
Gandhi sent a telegram hailing it as a first victory in India's struggle for freedom.

teach.h: 1922: GURU KA BAGH, NOT STRIKING BACK.
teach.b: Then came the road in the hook: Guru ka Bagh, 1922, the garden of a gurdwara near Amritsar. Day after day, bands of volunteers walked to cut wood, were beaten by police, and did not strike back. An English clergyman, C.

F. Andrews, went to see it, and wrote that he had witnessed something like a new heroism, born of suffering without retaliation. Thousands were arrested over those years; many were injured, and some died.
Then, in 1925, the government passed the Sikh Gurdwaras Act.

teach.h: 1925: AN ELECTED BODY FOR THE GURDWARAS.
teach.b: The historic gurdwaras of Punjab would be run by an elected Sikh body, which became the SGPC, and Sikh men and women would vote for it. It still runs the Harmandir and many other gurdwaras today.
The vow from Nankana Sahib had held for years, through beatings and prison.

how: The SGPC, elected by Sikh voters, manages the Harmandir Sahib and many historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring states; it also publishes the Sikh Rehat Maryada.

o: the Sikh political party that governs Punjab
the council of scholars who lead the Akal Takht
the elected Sikh body that runs historic gurdwaras

games.q: Guru ka Bagh, 1922. yesterday's volunteers were beaten on the road. it's your turn to walk. what do you do?
o: walk the same road, and don't strike back.
games.why: band after band walked and did not strike back. three years later, the gurdwaras were returned to the Sikhs.

practice: Think of something in your community that isn't right, small enough that one voice could count: at school, at work, in your town, in your place of worship.

Picture one peaceful, firm step: a vote, a letter, a respectful question at a meeting, your name signed to something, or simply saying out loud what you think. Choose one, and see yourself doing it calmly.

wordCard.voice: SGPC. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the elected Sikh body that took charge of the historic gurdwaras after years of peaceful protest.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: shiromani, foremost or supreme, the first word of SGPC.

carryVoice: Your line: peaceful protest worked. Years of beatings and prison, and then a law. One day to three hundred.
